passages.text: Lavandula angustifolia, formerly L. officinalis, is a flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean basin. Its common names include lavender, true lavender and English lavender (though it is not native to England); also garden lavender, common lavender and narrow-leaved lavender.

It is a strongly aromatic shrub growing as high as {{convert|1 to 2|m|ft|frac=2}} tall. The leaves are evergreen, {{convert|2|-|6|cm|frac=2|abbr=off}} long, and {{convert|4|-|6|mm|in|frac=16}} broad. The flowers are typically purple (lavender-coloured), produced on spikes {{convert|2|-|8|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long at the top of slender, leafless stems {{convert|10|-|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long.{{Citation needed|date=October 2024}}

Etymology
The species name angustifolia is Latin for "narrow leaf". Previously, it was known as Lavandula officinalis, referring to its medicinal properties.

Cultivation
English lavender is commonly grown as an ornamental plant. It is popular for its colourful flowers, its fragrance, and its ability to survive with low water consumption. It does not grow well in continuously damp soil and may benefit from increased drainage. It does best in Mediterranean climates similar to its native habitat, characterised by wet winters and dry summers. It is fairly tolerant of low temperatures, and is generally considered hardy to Royal Horticultural Society zone H6, or USDA zone 5. It tolerates acid soils, but favours neutral to alkaline soils, and in some conditions it may be short-lived.

Dwarf cultivars
{{More references|section|date=November 2025}}
Compacta, Folgate, Dwarf Blue, Dwarf White, Hidcote Pink, Hidcote Superior, Munstead, Nana Atropurpurea, Nana Rosea, Sarah, Summerland Supreme, Lady Lavender
'Hidcote Superior', a compact evergreen shrub {{convert|40 × 45|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} with fragrant gray-green foliage and deep violet-blue flowers in summer, prefers full sun, well drained soil, low water, hardy to {{convert|-30|°C|°F|abbr=on}}, western Mediterranean species
'Munstead' (syn. Dwarf Munstead, Munstead Blue and Munstead Variety) L. angustifolia variety, {{convert|30|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall, having pink-purple to lavender-blue inflorescences that are slightly fragrant, named after Munstead Wood in Surrey, which was the home of Gertrude Jekyll
'Sarah', grows to {{convert|15|–|60|cm|in|abbr=on}}, the flowers are petite, as is the plant, used as a short edging, or as a very fragrant addition to the window box, dark violet flowers
'Lady Lavender', grows to {{convert|45|cm|in|abbr=on}}, fragrant, gray-green foliage and lavender-blue flowers in summer, prefers full sun, well-drained soil, low water, hardy to {{convert|-30|°C|°F|abbr=on}}

Giant cultivars
{{Unreferenced|section|date=November 2025}}
Alba, Backhouse Purple, Biostos, Bridestowe, Graves, Gray Lady, Gwendolyn Anley, Hidcote Giant, Irene Doyle, Mailette, Middachten
'Hidcote Giant'. A Lavandula × intermedia lavandin. Very vigorous grower ({{convert|90|to|100|cm|in|abbr=on|disp=semicolon}}) with a lovely strong fragrance. This has large deep lavender-purple flowers on very long {{convert|60|cm|in|abbr=on}} stems.
'Vera' {{convert|75|to|90|cm|in|abbr=on}}. Thought to be the original species lavender, harvested for its oil.

The flowers and leaves are applied in herbal medicine. Commercially, the plant is used to produce lavender essential oil used in balms, salves, perfumes, cosmetics, and topical applications. Lavender essential oil, when diluted with a carrier oil, is commonly used for massage therapy or aromatherapy.
The flowers are also used as a culinary herb, most often as part of the North American version of the French herb blend called herbes de Provence.
Lavandula angustifolia is included in the Tasmanian Fire Service's list of low flammability plants, indicating that it is suitable for growing within a building protection zone.

Subspecies
Lavandula angustifolia subsp. angustifolia
Lavandula angustifolia subsp. pyrenaica

Hybrids
Lavandula hybrids are referred to as lavandins. Hybrids between L. angustifolia and L. latifolia (spike lavender) are called Lavandula × intermedia. They bloom later than the ordinary English lavenders.
